Leading AI Adoption: What Changed Inside Our Engineering Organization?
Press enter or click to view image in full size

AI adoption delivers real engineering value when speed is balanced with architecture, accountability, validation, and disciplined delivery.In my previous article, “Vibe Coding: Productivity Booster or Technical Debt Accelerator?”, I discussed how AI-assisted development can significantly improve engineering productivity, but only when combined with strong engineering discipline.
I had planned to move next into Agentic Engineering, but after publishing that article, several engineering leaders reached out with a different set of questions. Some really thought provoking interesting discussions. They weren’t asking which AI tool to use or how to write better prompts.
The questions were practical: How do you avoid inconsistent AI-generated implementations? How do you measure adoption without creating vanity metrics? How do you preserve accountability when code is generated faster than ever? And how do you make sure AI improves engineering quality instead of accelerating technical debt?
They wanted to know:
“What actually changes inside an engineering organization once AI becomes part of everyday software development?”
Having led the development of a cloud-native Pharmacovigilance (PV) platform, I thought I’d answer that question by sharing what changed for us, not just technically, but operationally.
In a regulated domain like pharmacovigilance, faster delivery only matters if traceability, validation, auditability, and quality remain intact.
The interesting part is that most of these changes had very little to do with AI itself.
They had everything to do with how we worked.
We Changed the Conversation Before We Changed the Code
One of our earliest realizations was that AI makes it very easy to jump straight into implementation.
Developers could describe a requirement, generate code within minutes, and immediately begin refining it.
Initially, that felt like a huge productivity boost.
But after a few sprints, we noticed a pattern.
Different developers were generating different implementations for similar problems. The code worked, but the approaches varied. During reviews, architects were spending more time discussing design consistency than reviewing the implementation itself.
The problem wasn’t AI.
The problem was that we were asking AI to solve problems before the team had agreed on the design.
So we changed our workflow.
Instead of asking:
“How should we implement this?”
we started asking:
“What is the right design for this capability?”
Only after agreeing on architecture, interfaces, and business workflows did we use AI to accelerate implementation.
That small shift had one of the biggest impacts on consistency across the project.
Our Definition of “Done” Quietly Changed
Before AI-assisted development, completing a feature usually meant writing code, testing it, and creating the necessary documentation.
Once AI became part of the workflow, another expectation emerged.
Every engineer needed to understand and justify the generated implementation.
During code reviews, a question naturally became part of our discussions:
“Can you explain why this implementation is correct?”
If the answer wasn’t clear, the feature wasn’t ready.
Not because AI had generated it.
Because engineering ownership still belonged to the developer.
AI could accelerate implementation.
It couldn’t own accountability.
JIRA Stories Became Less About Implementation
One unexpected change happened in our backlog.
Earlier, many JIRA stories naturally drifted toward implementation.
Examples included:
· Create REST endpoint
· Implement validation logic
· Build service for case processing
As AI became more capable of generating implementation, we realized these stories weren’t providing enough business context.
Instead, we started writing stories that emphasized:
· Business outcomes
· User workflows
· Acceptance criteria
· Regulatory considerations
· Non-functional requirements
· Architectural constraints
The implementation became more flexible because the intent became much clearer.
Interestingly, this also improved conversations between product managers, architects, and developers.
Everyone was discussing the customer problem instead of individual coding tasks.
Documentation Became a Strategic Asset
If there’s one lesson that surprised me the most, it was this:
AI increased the value of documentation.
Initially, some team members assumed documentation would become less important because AI could generate code and documentation automatically.
We experienced exactly the opposite.
The quality of AI-generated output improved dramatically when engineers had access to:
· Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
· API standards
· Coding guidelines
· Domain terminology
· Product workflows
· Design documents
Documentation stopped being something we created after development.
It became context that enabled better engineering decisions.
One sentence became part of many of our discussions:
AI is only as good as the context we provide.
Looking back, that realization feels like an early precursor to what we now recognize as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and enterprise knowledge engineering.
We Measured Outcomes, Not AI Usage
Several leaders asked whether we introduced new metrics to measure AI adoption.
The answer is no.
I wasn’t interested in measuring:
· Number of prompts
· Percentage of AI-generated code
· AI usage across teams
Those metrics might indicate adoption.
They don’t indicate value.
Instead, we kept focusing on outcomes.
The discussions became:
· Are we reducing lead time?
· Are code reviews becoming faster without compromising quality?
· Are developers spending more time solving business problems?
· Is onboarding becoming easier?
· Are production defects increasing or decreasing?
· Are we reaching customer feedback sooner?
Technology adoption should never become the objective.
Better product delivery should.
Validation Became More Important, Not Less
Because our platform supported pharmacovigilance processes, software quality and validation were already central to how we engineered the platform.
AI didn’t change that.
In fact, it reinforced it.
Every implementation still passed through:
· Peer review
· Automated testing
· Security validation
· Integration testing
· Regression testing
· Business workflow validation
One principle guided every discussion:
We validate software, not who or what wrote it.
Whether the first draft came from a developer or AI was irrelevant.
The quality bar remained exactly the same.
The Biggest Lesson Wasn’t About AI
Looking back, I don’t think AI exposed weaknesses in software engineering.
It exposed weaknesses in engineering practices.
Teams with:
· Clear architecture
· Strong coding standards
· Good documentation
· Healthy review culture
· Mature CI/CD pipelines
became more productive because AI accelerated practices that were already disciplined.
Teams with inconsistent engineering practices became inconsistent faster.
AI didn’t create our engineering culture.
It amplified it.
That may be the most important lesson from our adoption journey.
What I’d Recommend to Engineering Leaders
Based on that experience, these are the practices I would encourage engineering leaders to focus on:
· Align on design before generating implementation.
· Make explainability part of code review.
· Rewrite backlog items around intent and outcomes.
· Treat documentation as AI context, not project overhead.
· Measure delivery quality, not AI usage.
· Keep validation standards unchanged.
Looking Ahead
Our experience on the PV platform convinced me that AI-assisted development is a valuable evolution.
But it also made me realize something else.
We were still thinking about AI as a tool used by developers.
Today, I’d ask a different question.
What if AI wasn’t just helping engineers build the product?
What if AI became part of the product itself?
If I were designing that same Pharmacovigilance platform today, I wouldn’t stop at AI-assisted development.
I’d explore literature surveillance agents that continuously monitor scientific publications, signal detection agents that identify emerging safety trends, engineering agents that assist with incident investigation, and domain-aware assistants that help users navigate complex workflows.
That’s no longer about developer productivity.
It’s about reimagining how software creates value.
That’s the journey we’ll begin in the next article as we explore Agentic Engineering, not as a technology trend, but as the next evolution in building intelligent products.
